```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ggplot2)
```

fMRI noise is autocorrelated: what the scanner records at one volume
predicts part of what it records at the next. Ordinary least squares (OLS)
ignores this. Its coefficient estimates remain unbiased, but its standard
errors come out too small. Its *t* statistics are then too large, and a 5%
threshold passes more than 5% of the voxels that have no real effect.

Prewhitening fixes this. Estimate the autocorrelation from the residuals of
a first OLS fit, and build a filter that turns the noise into white noise,
meaning noise with no autocorrelation. Pass both the data and the design
matrix through that filter, then fit again. fmriAR does the estimation and
the filtering. This vignette works through the steps on simulated data,
where the right answers are known, so every result can be checked.

## A simulated study

The study has two five-minute runs of 150 volumes each, at a repetition time
(TR) of 2 seconds. The task is a series of brief events 12 to 20 seconds
apart, convolved with a canonical haemodynamic response. As in most fMRI
models, the design also has an intercept and three slow cosine drift terms
for each run.

```{r design}
library(fmriAR)
set.seed(2024)

TR <- 2
n_per_run <- 150
runs <- rep(1:2, each = n_per_run)   # a run label for every volume
n_time <- length(runs)

# Brief events 12-20 s apart, convolved with a canonical HRF
hrf <- function(t) dgamma(t, 6) - dgamma(t, 16) / 6
h <- hrf(seq(0, 30, by = TR))
event_regressor <- function(n) {
  onsets <- cumsum(sample(6:10, n, replace = TRUE))
  stim <- tabulate(onsets[onsets <= n], nbins = n)
  x <- stats::filter(stim, h / max(h), sides = 1)
  as.numeric(replace(x, is.na(x), 0))
}

# Three slow cosines per run absorb scanner drift
cosines <- function(n, k) {
  sapply(seq_len(k), function(j) cos(pi * j * (seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n))
}
none <- matrix(0, n_per_run, 3)

X <- cbind(c(event_regressor(n_per_run), event_regressor(n_per_run)),
           runs == 1, runs == 2,
           rbind(cosines(n_per_run, 3), none),
           rbind(none, cosines(n_per_run, 3)))
colnames(X) <- c("task", "run1", "run2", paste0("drift", 1:6))
```

The noise in each voxel is a first-order autoregressive process, AR(1), with
coefficient 0.5: each volume's noise is half the previous volume's plus a
fresh random shock. Each run is simulated separately, so no noise carries
over from one run to the next. One voxel in ten responds to the task. The
other 9,000 are *null voxels*, with no effect at all; counting how many of
them pass a threshold gives the false-positive rate.

```{r data}
n_vox <- 10000
active <- 1:1000
null <- setdiff(seq_len(n_vox), active)

ar1_run <- function() as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.5), n = n_per_run))
noise <- replicate(n_vox, c(ar1_run(), ar1_run()))

beta <- ifelse(seq_len(n_vox) %in% active, 0.5, 0)
Y <- noise + outer(X[, "task"], beta)
```

## The problem: OLS on autocorrelated noise

Fit OLS to every voxel and compute a *t* statistic for the task. Given the
unwhitened design and data, `sandwich_from_whitened_resid()` returns the
ordinary OLS standard errors.

```{r ols}
ols <- lm.fit(X, Y)
se_ols <- sandwich_from_whitened_resid(X, Y, beta = ols$coefficients)$se
t_ols <- ols$coefficients["task", ] / se_ols[1, ]

# Share of null voxels that pass |t| > 1.96
mean(abs(t_ols[null]) > 1.96)
```

```{r fpr-ols, include = FALSE}
fpr_ols <- mean(abs(t_ols[null]) > 1.96)
```

The threshold promises 5%. OLS delivers `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * fpr_ols)`.

## Step 1: Estimate the noise model

`fit_noise()` estimates the autocorrelation from the OLS residuals and fits
an autoregressive model to it. By default it chooses the model order by the
Bayesian information criterion, BIC (`p = "auto"`), and pools all voxels and
runs into one model (`pooling = "global"`). It never pairs a volume in one
run with a volume in another.

```{r fit}
plan <- fit_noise(ols$residuals, runs = runs, design = X)
plan
```

The result is a whitening *plan*: the fitted noise model, in the form
`whiten_apply()` takes. BIC chose AR(1) and estimated its coefficient at
`r sprintf("%.2f", plan$phi[[1]][1])`; the truth is 0.5.

Pass `design = X` whenever the residuals come from a fitted model. Fitting
removes some of the noise along with the effects being modelled, so the
residuals look less autocorrelated than the noise really is. The bias grows
with the size of the design, and drift terms cause most of it. `design = X`
corrects it. Without the correction, a fit that pools thousands of voxels can
also choose an AR order that is too high. *Refining the noise model*
(`vignette("fmriAR-noise-models")`) demonstrates both problems.

## Step 2: Whiten the design and the data

`whiten_apply()` runs the filter down every column of `X` and `Y`,
restarting it at the beginning of each run. It returns whitened copies and
leaves your inputs unchanged.

```{r whiten}
w <- whiten_apply(plan, X, Y, runs = runs)
```

For an AR(1), the filter is a single subtraction: each whitened value is the
original value minus `r sprintf("%.2f", plan$phi[[1]][1])` times the value
one volume earlier. That removes the part of the noise the previous volume
predicts and leaves the fresh shock. The first volume of each run has no
predecessor, so instead it is multiplied by $\sqrt{1 - \phi^2}$, where
$\phi$ is the AR coefficient. That makes the result exact generalised least
squares (GLS).

The design must go through the same filter. The model says data = design
× coefficients + noise. Filtering both sides with the same filter leaves the
equation, and its coefficients, intact; only the noise changes, and it
becomes white.

```{r fig-filter, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.9, fig.cap = "The task regressor before (grey) and after (blue) whitening, volumes 40 to 100 of run 1. Each blue value is the grey value minus half the grey value one volume earlier. Every voxel's data goes through the same filter."}
win <- 40:100
fd <- data.frame(t = win, before = X[win, "task"], after = w$X[win, "task"])
pk <- win[which.max(fd$before)]                 # label beside the tallest peak
ggplot(fd, aes(t)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_line(aes(y = before), colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = after, colour = "Whitened"), linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = pk + 1.3, y = fd$before[fd$t == pk], label = "before",
           hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = "grey45") +
  annotate("text", x = pk - 1.5, y = fd$after[fd$t == pk - 1],
           label = "whitened", hjust = 1, size = 3.1) +
  albersdown::scale_color_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Volume (TR = 2 s)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

The whitened regressor rises earlier and falls faster than the original,
and dips below zero after each response. Whitening keeps the changes in a
signal and discounts its slow, sustained parts, because slow fluctuations
are exactly what autocorrelated noise produces on its own.

## Step 3: Refit and compute standard errors

Fit the whitened data on the whitened design. Once the noise is white, the
ordinary standard-error formula is the right one.

```{r refit}
gls <- lm.fit(w$X, w$Y)
se_gls <- sandwich_from_whitened_resid(w$X, w$Y, beta = gls$coefficients)$se
t_gls <- gls$coefficients["task", ] / se_gls[1, ]
```

Because the simulation records which voxels have an effect, each fit can be
scored against the truth. Over the 9,000 null voxels, the *reported*
standard error should match the *actual* spread of the estimates, and 5% of
the voxels should pass the threshold. The last column, the share of the
1,000 active voxels that pass, measures sensitivity.

```{r compare}
summarise_fit <- function(b, se) {
  c(`reported SE`    = mean(se[1, null]),
    `actual SD`      = sd(b["task", null]),
    `false positive` = mean(abs(b["task", null] / se[1, null]) > 1.96),
    `true positive`  = mean(abs(b["task", active] / se[1, active]) > 1.96))
}
knitr::kable(
  rbind(OLS = summarise_fit(ols$coefficients, se_ols),
        prewhitened = summarise_fit(gls$coefficients, se_gls)),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The task effect estimated by OLS and after prewhitening, scored against the simulation's truth."
)
```

OLS reports a standard error well below the actual spread of its estimates,
and its false-positive rate more than doubles. After prewhitening, reported
and actual agree, and the rate is back near 5%. The whitened estimates also
vary less than the OLS ones, so little real sensitivity is lost: much of
OLS's higher true-positive rate came from the same too-small standard error
that produced its false positives.

In relative terms, the excess grows as the threshold tightens. OLS passes
about twice the nominal rate at 5%, and several times the nominal rate at
0.1%, the kind of strict threshold that whole-brain analyses use.

```{r alpha-table}
rejection_rate <- function(t, alpha) mean(abs(t[null]) > qnorm(1 - alpha / 2))
alpha <- c(0.05, 0.01, 0.001)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * x)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(threshold = pct(alpha),
             OLS = pct(sapply(alpha, rejection_rate, t = t_ols)),
             prewhitened = pct(sapply(alpha, rejection_rate, t = t_gls))),
  align = "rrr",
  caption = "Share of null voxels declared significant at each threshold."
)
```

The distribution of the null *t* statistics shows where the excess comes
from. Under OLS it is wider than the standard normal that the threshold
assumes; after whitening it matches.

```{r fig-null, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "The task t statistic in the 9,000 null voxels. The curve is the standard normal distribution that a valid test assumes. Orange bars, where |t| > 1.96, are false positives."}
n_null <- length(null)
fpr <- c(mean(abs(t_ols[null]) > 1.96), mean(abs(t_gls[null]) > 1.96))
lev <- c(sprintf("OLS: %.1f%% of null voxels pass |t| > 1.96", 100 * fpr[1]),
         sprintf("Whitened: %.1f%% (a valid test gives 5%%)", 100 * fpr[2]))
tn <- data.frame(fit = factor(rep(lev, each = n_null), levels = lev),
                 t = c(t_ols[null], t_gls[null]))
tn$tail <- ifelse(abs(tn$t) > 1.96, "false positive", "inside")
bw <- 1.96 / 7                    # a bin edge sits exactly on the threshold
curve <- data.frame(t = seq(-5, 5, by = 0.02))
curve$d <- dnorm(curve$t)
curve_lab <- data.frame(fit = factor(lev[1], levels = lev), t = 1.15, d = 0.36,
                        txt = "standard normal:\nwhat a valid test gives")
ggplot(tn, aes(t)) +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(tn, tail == "inside"),
                 aes(y = after_stat(count / (n_null * bw))),
                 binwidth = bw, boundary = 0, fill = "grey78") +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(tn, tail == "false positive"),
                 aes(y = after_stat(count / (n_null * bw)), fill = "OLS"),
                 binwidth = bw, boundary = 0) +
  geom_line(data = curve, aes(t, d), colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(data = curve_lab, aes(t, d, label = txt), hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
            size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.95, colour = "grey25") +
  facet_wrap(~fit, ncol = 1) +
  albersdown::scale_fill_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-1.96, 0, 1.96), labels = c("-1.96", "0", "1.96")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-5, 5), ylim = c(0, 0.45)) +
  labs(x = "t statistic, no-effect voxels", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```

## Step 4: The whiteness check

If the filter matches the noise, the residuals of the whitened fit are white:
a voxel's residual at one volume says nothing about its residual at the next.
`acorr_diagnostics()` measures each voxel's autocorrelation at lags 1, 2, …,
centring each run separately and never pairing volumes across a run boundary.

```{r acf}
resid_w <- w$Y - w$X %*% gls$coefficients
ac_before <- acorr_diagnostics(ols$residuals, runs = runs, max_lag = 10,
                               aggregate = "none")
ac_after <- acorr_diagnostics(resid_w, runs = runs, max_lag = 10,
                              aggregate = "none")

# Share of voxels whose lag-1 autocorrelation falls outside the
# white-noise band, +/- ci
c(before = mean(abs(ac_before$acf[1, ]) > ac_before$ci),
  after  = mean(abs(ac_after$acf[1, ]) > ac_after$ci))
```

`ci` is $1.96 / \sqrt{n}$, where $n$ is the number of volumes. A white-noise
series keeps 95% of its autocorrelations within $\pm$`ci`, the *white-noise
band*. The band describes one voxel, so compare it with the spread of
autocorrelations across voxels, not with their average, which varies far
less. Before whitening, every voxel's lag-1 autocorrelation lies outside the
band. After whitening,
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(abs(ac_after$acf[1, ]) > ac_after$ci))` do,
close to the 5% expected of white noise.

```{r fig-acf, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Autocorrelation of each voxel's residuals at lags 1 to 10, after OLS (left) and after whitening (right). Lines span the middle 95% of the 10,000 voxels; dots mark the median. The grey band is where 95% of one voxel's values fall if its noise is white."}
acf_summary <- function(a, stage) {
  data.frame(stage = stage, lag = a$lags,
             lo = apply(a$acf, 1, quantile, 0.025),
             mid = apply(a$acf, 1, median),
             hi = apply(a$acf, 1, quantile, 0.975))
}
lev <- c("OLS", "Whitened")
acs <- rbind(acf_summary(ac_before, lev[1]), acf_summary(ac_after, lev[2]))
acs$stage <- factor(acs$stage, levels = lev)
ci <- ac_after$ci
band_lab <- data.frame(stage = factor(lev[2], levels = lev), lag = 10.4, y = ci,
                       txt = "white-noise range")
ggplot(acs, aes(lag)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -ci, ymax = ci,
           fill = "grey88") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, colour = stage), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mid, colour = stage), size = 1.8) +
  geom_text(data = band_lab, aes(lag, y, label = txt), hjust = 1, vjust = -0.5,
            size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~stage) +
  albersdown::scale_color_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Lag (volumes)", y = "Autocorrelation") +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

The whitened autocorrelations centre slightly below zero, at about
`r sprintf("%.2f", median(ac_after$acf))`. That is expected: fitting a model
makes its residuals slightly negatively autocorrelated, and the more
regressors per run, the larger the shift. The same shift is why the share
outside the band is a little above 5%.

If some autocorrelation remains, for example because the AR order was too
low, `sandwich_from_whitened_resid(..., type = "hac", runs = runs)` gives
standard errors that tolerate it (Newey–West, computed within runs).

## Common situations

### Several runs

`pooling = "global"` (the default) fits one noise model to all runs.
`pooling = "run"` gives each run its own coefficients, which suits runs that
differ in length or acquisition.

```{r pooling-run}
plan_by_run <- fit_noise(ols$residuals, runs = runs, design = X,
                         pooling = "run")
plan_by_run$phi
```

### Censored volumes

Pass volumes flagged for motion (scrubbed volumes) as `censor`, either as
indices or as a logical vector with one entry per volume. They are left out
of the noise estimate, and the filter restarts after each one so that no
flagged value leaks into its neighbours. The whitened output keeps every row
and lists the censored rows in `censor`; drop them before fitting.

```{r censor}
scrub <- c(50:52, 170)
plan_c <- fit_noise(ols$residuals, runs = runs, design = X, censor = scrub)
w_c <- whiten_apply(plan_c, X, Y, runs = runs)

keep <- setdiff(seq_len(n_time), w_c$censor)
fit_c <- lm.fit(w_c$X[keep, ], w_c$Y[keep, ])
```

`whiten_apply()` reuses the plan's censored volumes when the data have the
length the plan was fitted on, as here; otherwise pass `censor` yourself.

### One call

`whiten()` fits the OLS model, estimates the noise model and whitens, all in
one step. Arguments after `censor`, such as `design` here, go to
`fit_noise()`.

```{r one-call}
w1 <- whiten(X, Y, runs = runs, design = X)
```

### Large data

Whitening runs in parallel over voxels when fmriAR is built with OpenMP.
`options(fmriAR.max_threads = k)` caps the number of threads.
